routes.description: Establish a cumulative route from libertarian agency and a caused temporal universe to a divine agent, then use historical resurrection claims to identify that agent with the Christian God while addressing hiddenness and revelation objections.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its generic theistic arguments warrant a personal divine cause, the resurrection inference supplies a specifically Christian identification, and the principal skeptical challenges do not defeat the cumulative evidential connection.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative philosophical and historical case to the existence of the specifically Christian God rather than merely an unspecified cause or deity.

centralBridges.description: Show that libertarian agency is real, required for rational and moral responsibility, and better explained by theism than by naturalistic determinism.
Show that the universe began to exist and that its cause is a timeless, immaterial, powerful agent rather than an unspecified impersonal condition.
Show that the relevant historical claims are adequately grounded and that divine resurrection explains them better than the principal naturalistic alternatives.
Explain why the available evidence and mode of divine disclosure are compatible with a Christian God seeking freely formed trust.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend philosophical and historical inference as legitimate methods for realities and past events not directly measurable by scientific instruments.
Preserve the supporting credibility of transmitted Christian sources and reported miracles against claims of pervasive corruption or evidential disappearance.

routes.description: Withhold belief in the Christian God by testing each component of the cumulative case for reliable support, Christian specificity, and explanatory discrimination, while treating hiddenness and inconsistent revelation as contrary evidence.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if libertarian agency, the divine Kalam extension, and resurrection remain insufficiently established or non-unique, and if the expected clarity and consistency of Christian revelation are absent under reliable evidential standards.

motionBridge.description: Show that the offered arguments do not warrant belief in the specifically Christian God and that skepticism need not establish universal divine nonexistence.

centralBridges.description: Challenge both the evidence for libertarian freedom and its compatibility with an omniscient creator who knowingly selects a complete world history.
Separate the claim that the universe has a cause from unsupported conclusions that the cause is an agent, a God, or the Christian God.
Require historical and supernatural claims to rest on confirmable evidence and methods capable of distinguishing resurrection or divinity from natural, technological, or deceptive alternatives.
Show that sincere nonbelief, unclear disclosure, competing revelations, and textual uncertainty conflict with expectations generated by the proposed Christian God.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Ground rational skepticism in provisional confidence and claim-sensitive evidence without requiring absolute certainty or asserting the disputed proposition is false.
Test whether faith, philosophical inference, historical comparison, and miracle reports reliably discriminate true Christian claims from incompatible alternatives.

sections.title: Libertarian Freedom, Rational Agency, and Divine Foreknowledge
sections.rationale: This issue tests a foundational argument for God from experienced freedom, moral responsibility, and rational deliberation, together with the objection that libertarian choice is unverified or incompatible with divine creation and foreknowledge.

sections.title: Kalam and the Identity of the Universe's Cause
sections.rationale: This issue covers both the inference that the universe requires a cause and the further bridge from a temporal beginning to a timeless personal agent, including whether those added attributes uniquely support theism.

sections.title: Resurrection Evidence and Christian Identification
sections.rationale: The resurrection is the principal bridge from generic theistic considerations to the specifically Christian God, making the status of the historical premises, alternative explanations, and antecedent miracle plausibility central to the motion.

sections.title: Divine Hiddenness, Revelation, and Textual Reliability
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether sincere nonbelief, religious disagreement, ambiguous disclosure, and manuscript uncertainty count against the expected conduct of the Christian God or remain compatible with freely chosen trust and preserved revelation.

sections.title: Evidential Standards, Falsifiability, and Explanatory Discrimination
sections.rationale: This cross-cutting issue determines which philosophical, historical, empirical, and testimonial methods can warrant extraordinary conclusions and whether observed anomalies can discriminate divine action from unknown or deceptive alternatives.

moves.speaker: Braxton Hunter
moves.proposition: The libertarian freedom people experience is better explained by God because a natural universe operating solely through physical cause and effect would be deterministic.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly introduces Hunter, and the uninterrupted first-person opening statement presents his announced affirmative case.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly advances the central libertarian-agency bridge by offering theism as an explanation of experienced alternative possibilities.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it states a clear explanatory thesis but compresses both the evidence for libertarian freedom and the naturalism-to-determinism bridge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The thesis is recoverable, but “natural system,” determinism, and the scope of physical causation are not sufficiently distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling God the best explanation and appealing to what everyone knows substantially exceeds the supplied experiential and conceptual support.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference depends on an underdefended dichotomy between natural physical causation and libertarian agency, plus an implicit explanatory bridge to God.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The principal support is introspective confidence that people could do otherwise; no representative evidence or serious rival comparison is supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It contacts the indispensable libertarian-agency bridge directly, though it does not complete the evidential and comparative requirements of that bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents its affirmative explanation without materially characterizing a developed opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says a natural universe would be a system of cause and effect, that God could grant libertarian freedom, and that people know they could do otherwise.

moves.speaker: Braxton Hunter
moves.proposition: Because the universe began to exist, its cause must transcend space, time, and matter and is best identified as a sufficiently powerful disembodied mind.
moves.attributionBasis: Hunter explicitly introduces his second argument and develops the Kalam syllogism and his inference about the nature of its cause.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly advances the central cosmic-cause bridge by deriving a transcendent cause and identifying it as a disembodied mind.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it supplies a recognizable causal route but leaves the decisive transition from transcendence to mentality compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The causal thesis is clear, but the extent to which timelessness, immateriality, power, and mentality follow is insufficiently qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Necessary causal attributes and the mental identification are asserted with more force than the stated Kalam premises independently warrant.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The basic cause inference is usable, but the move leaves a material bridge from a cause outside physical spacetime to a personal disembodied mind.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A standard causal syllogism and constituent analysis are offered, but support for the universe’s beginning and serious causal alternatives is compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly targets the central requirement to identify the universe’s cause, while leaving the personal-agent portion materially underderived.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops its preferred cause without engaging a sufficiently specified live impersonal-cause alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that whatever begins has an external cause, applies this to the universe, and reasons from time, space, and matter not causing themselves.

moves.speaker: Braxton Hunter
moves.proposition: The disciples' reported experiences and willingness to die for their proclamation are better explained by God raising Jesus than by deliberate fabrication or disputed visionary-error accounts.
moves.attributionBasis: Hunter marks this as the third historical consideration and concludes by synthesizing the facts into his resurrection inference.

response.rationale: This constructive move advances the central resurrection bridge by comparing resurrection with fabrication and visionary-error explanations.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it reaches the key explanatory comparison, but the historical grounding and antecedent-probability recalibration remain compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The best-explanation thesis and principal comparison are clear, with an implicit dependence on the earlier minimal-facts and plausibility qualifications.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move acknowledges disputed miracle plausibility, but “easily” the best hypothesis modestly exceeds the abbreviated comparative defense shown.

charity.alternative: The disciples’ reports could reflect sincere visionary or interpretive error rather than deliberate fabrication.
charity.decisiveQualification: Sincerity and willingness to suffer exclude simple fraud more readily than they exclude sincere nonresurrection explanations.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive structure is coherent, but the inference compresses the bridge from sincere reported experiences and risk-taking to a uniquely divine resurrection.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move cites reported experiences and willingness to die, yet the underlying historical documentation, independence, and broader rival comparison remain underdeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the central resurrection-explanation requirement and compares principal alternatives, although it does not fully secure the historical premises.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes fabrication and visionary-error rivals, though it treats the sincerity evidence as more discriminating than it clearly is.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes willingness to die, disputes the antecedent dismissal of miracles through recalibrated plausibility, and concludes that God raising Jesus is the best explanation.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Arguments equally available to multiple religions cannot establish the specifically Christian God, and skepticism need not assert that every god is nonexistent.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker follows Hunter's completed opener, identifies Hunter by name, and states the skeptical position associated with Dillahunty.

components.text: Whether the resurrection inference actually identifies the specifically Christian God rather than supporting only generic supernatural agency.
Whether the Kalam-derived cause supplies specifically Christian rather than religion-neutral identification.
Whether the freedom explanation distinguishes Christianity from other religious explanations.

response.rationale: The move contacts the cumulative case’s specificity demand across all three earlier arguments, but it does not directly defeat the resurrection evidence itself.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer that squarely contacts Christian specificity while leaving the historical merits of the resurrection inference substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between generic God arguments and specifically Christian warrant is explicit and consistently scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that religion-neutral arguments cannot alone establish Christianity matches the logical support and is properly qualified.

charity.alternative: The resurrection argument may supplement generic theism and provide the specifically Christian identification missing from the first two arguments.
charity.decisiveQualification: That possibility must be assessed on the resurrection evidence rather than dismissed merely because the philosophical arguments are shared.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The specificity inference is valid and the distinction between withholding belief and proving universal nonexistence is clear, with only a bounded application gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Religious portability is illustrated with multiple traditions, but the claim’s application to the distinct resurrection component is not yet demonstrated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the motion-level requirement that the cumulative case establish the specifically Christian God rather than an unspecified deity.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move anticipates that more will be said but initially groups the case broadly, leaving the resurrection’s intended identifying role underexamined.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says arguments equally viable for Hindu, Sikh, Muslim, or Jewish views are not specifically Christian and clarifies that skepticism is not undertaking to disprove God.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: A specified God model generates observable expectations from its attributed goals and conduct, so the absence of those expected conditions provides disconfirming evidence.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted first-person skeptical presentation and explicit introduction of divine hiddenness identify Dillahunty as speaker.

response.rationale: This constructive move establishes a predictive framework for the central hiddenness-and-revelation bridge by comparing attributed divine goals with observed conditions.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it supplies a disciplined model-to-prediction method, though the actual Christian predictions and observations remain only partly specified.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional method is clear: specify a God model, derive expectations, and treat their absence as model-relative evidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move frames missing predictions as disconfirming rather than conclusive and makes the result conditional on specified divine attributes and goals.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The predictive-evidential structure is coherent and appropriately conditional, with a bounded missing bridge concerning which observations the Christian model specifically predicts.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The method is well motivated conceptually, but the excerpt supplies limited representative observations and no detailed likelihood comparison between models.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central hiddenness bridge by specifying how divine goals generate testable expectations, though application remains incomplete.

representationalCharity.rationale: This methodological constructive does not yet characterize a developed theistic account of why expected disclosure might be limited.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks that a God model’s characteristics, goals, interactions, and wants be defined so predictions can be compared with what reality contains.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Competing religious revelations and sincere unanswered seeking show that nonbelief can be reasonable rather than the product of dishonesty or culpable resistance.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained autobiographical skeptical argument and references to Matt in the third person by imagined critics securely identify Dillahunty.

response.rationale: This constructive move advances the central revelation bridge through competing claims and a concrete case of sincere seeking without the expected divine response.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it provides directly relevant contrary experience but relies heavily on autobiography and compresses the broader religious-disagreement evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: Reasonable sincere nonbelief is recoverable, but the move’s transition from personal experience to the wider class of seekers is only implicitly limited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The personal case is offered to show that reasonable nonbelief can occur, a modest conclusion that fits the acknowledged experiential basis.

charity.alternative: A sincere seeker may fail to perceive a divine response even if God provides evidence through other means or on another timetable.
charity.decisiveQualification: That possibility does not by itself show culpable resistance or remove the evidential tension created by sincere unmet seeking.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument coherently supports the possibility of reasonable nonbelief, though a material generalization bridge remains between one sincere report and broader revelation claims.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The central support is sincere autobiographical testimony, with competing revelations and representative external evidence asserted more than documented in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Sincere unanswered seeking directly contacts the central hiddenness-and-revelation requirement, while the competing-revelation portion is less fully evidenced.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move leaves room for model-dependent expectations and uses the autobiography mainly against blanket accusations of dishonesty or resistance.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes applying skepticism to one’s own Christianity and sincerely seeking divine help while expecting a real God to respond.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Even extraordinary phenomena would not uniquely establish God unless a reliable method could distinguish divinity from advanced intelligence, deception, or mentalist trickery.
moves.attributionBasis: First-person references to being a magician, mentalist, former Christian, and skeptic align unambiguously with Dillahunty's presentation.

response.rationale: This constructive move supports the subsidiary method-reliability bridge by demanding a method that distinguishes divinity from advanced or deceptive agency.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly articulates the discrimination requirement and supplies concrete rival-source examples, though no positive test is developed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is explicitly limited to non-unique confirmation: impressive phenomena alone do not identify their source as divine.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Requiring source discrimination for unique divine identification is proportionate to the logical underdetermination the examples demonstrate.

charity.alternative: An extraordinary event could still provide substantial evidence for God even if it did not deductively exclude every advanced or deceptive source.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move challenges unique confirmation, not necessarily all incremental evidential force from an extraordinary event.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The underdetermination inference is explicit, consistent, and supported by relevant alternative causes; it does not confuse unexplained phenomena with proof of God.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Advanced-intelligence and mentalist examples concretely support non-uniqueness, with only a bounded gap about how representative such alternatives would be.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly contacts the subsidiary reliability bridge by defining a discrimination test, but does not itself resolve a central historical claim.

representationalCharity.rationale: The examples fairly preserve the possibility of impressive evidence while insisting that impressive performance does not by itself identify divinity.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says even powerful linguistic phenomena would not confirm God without distinguishing God from advanced intelligence, magic, or mentalist performance.

moves.speaker: Braxton Hunter
moves.proposition: The resurrection case supplements the generic arguments for a creator by identifying the inferred God specifically as the Christian God.
moves.attributionBasis: Hunter continues the same rebuttal and explicitly describes the sequence and intended function of his own opening arguments.

components.text: Whether any part of the cumulative case identifies the inferred deity specifically with Christianity.

response.rationale: The move directly answers the specificity objection by assigning generic-theism work to the first two arguments and Christian identification to the resurrection case.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This full answer explicitly contacts the decisive specificity premise, although it identifies the intended bridge more clearly than it proves the bridge succeeds.

precisionFindings.rationale: The roles of the generic arguments and the resurrection argument are distinctly and explicitly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move modestly clarifies what the resurrection case was brought to demonstrate without claiming that clarification alone settles its evidential merits.

charity.alternative: The specificity objection may concern whether the resurrection evidence succeeds, not merely whether Hunter intended it to identify Christianity.
charity.decisiveQualification: Clarifying the cumulative architecture answers omission of a Christian bridge but does not independently validate the resurrection inference.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The cumulative division of labor is coherent and directly resolves the claim that every component must independently be Christian-specific, with one evidential bridge left open.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The reply accurately points to the resurrection component, but largely states its intended identifying function rather than adding support for that function.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the motion-level Christian-identification bridge by explaining where the specifically Christian inference enters the cumulative case.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly recognizes the generic-versus-Christian distinction, though it answers the architectural reading more fully than the evidential reading.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes the first two arguments as arguments that God exists and says the resurrection case was offered to show that the God at issue is Christian.

moves.speaker: Braxton Hunter
moves.proposition: God is not substantially hidden because evidence is widely available, while limited disclosure permits the freely chosen trust and loyalty God seeks rather than mere intellectual acknowledgment.
moves.attributionBasis: Hunter explicitly identifies Matt's divine-hiddenness argument and answers it throughout the uninterrupted remainder of this rebuttal segment.

components.text: Whether the Christian God’s goals predict more unmistakable public evidence than is observed.
Whether sincere nonbelief and unmet seeking remain compatible with God’s aim of freely formed trust.

response.rationale: The reply contacts both hiddenness demands by replacing mere acknowledgment with freely chosen trust as the relevant predicted divine goal.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts the decisive goal-prediction component but does not substantiate the optimal-evidence claim or directly explain competing revelations.

precisionFindings.rationale: The trust-versus-acknowledgment distinction is clear, but claims about available evidence and the greatest freely trusting population are insufficiently scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The assertion that this evidential level optimizes freely chosen relationship is speculative and presented without an explicit uncertainty qualification.

charity.alternative: Clear evidence of existence may permit rather than coerce free trust, since acknowledgment and relational loyalty are distinct choices.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply distinguishes belief from trust but must still show why clearer existence evidence would undermine the latter.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between acknowledgment and trust is coherent, but the inference that limited evidence maximizes free relationship rests on a substantial unsupported conditional.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The optimal-disclosure claim is largely speculative and lacks comparative evidence about how differing clarity would affect trust, loyalty, or sincere nonbelief.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central hiddenness prediction by revising the divine-goal model, while leaving inconsistent revelation and optimization underdeveloped.

representationalCharity.rationale: It recognizes the intellectual-belief issue but omits the strongest qualification that clearer evidence need not compel loyalty or relationship.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says God seeks trust and loyalty rather than mere intellectual belief and suggests the existing amount of evidence enables the greatest number to respond freely.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Libertarian freedom is unverified and conflicts with a creator who foreknows and selects the universe's complete history while exercising providence and issuing prophecy.
moves.attributionBasis: A clear post-rebuttal speaker transition precedes first-person references to compatibilism and direct responses to Hunter's opening claims.

components.text: Whether the felt ability to do otherwise verifies actual libertarian alternative possibilities.
Whether libertarian freedom coheres with an omniscient creator selecting a complete world history.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges both the evidence for alternative possibilities and their compatibility with classical divine foreknowledge and creation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This full answer explicitly contacts the experiential premise and adds a distinct internal-coherence objection to the proposed theistic explanation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly separates the epistemic challenge to libertarian freedom from the compatibility challenge involving the creator model.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The verification challenge is proportionate, but describing a direct conflict slightly outruns the abbreviated modal argument in the excerpt.

charity.alternative: Foreknowledge may track a free choice without causing it, and divine selection may preserve agent-dependent counterfactual freedom.
charity.decisiveQualification: Noncausation alone does not resolve whether selecting a fully foreknown history leaves relevant alternatives genuinely available.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The two-pronged challenge is coherent, but the incompatibility inference requires a fuller modal bridge distinguishing certainty, causation, and world selection.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The inability to verify otherwise-possibilities is a material evidential challenge; the providence and prophecy claims receive less detailed support here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central libertarian-agency bridge at both its experiential premise and its compatibility with the proposed God.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move targets foreknowledge plus world selection rather than merely confusing knowledge with efficient causation, though the modal alternatives are compressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks how an impression of being able to do otherwise differs from the fact and argues that classical omniscience conflicts with libertarian freedom.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: The Kalam concludes only that the universe has a cause; identifying that cause as a transcendent agent or God adds assertions not derived by the syllogism.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty explicitly turns to Hunter's Kalam argument and continues analyzing its premises, conclusion, and added divine interpretation through the context boundary.

components.text: Whether the Kalam syllogism derives a transcendent personal agent rather than only some cause of the universe.

response.rationale: The reply identifies the syllogism’s limited conclusion, locates the added divine attributes outside it, and states that the intended God-identification does not follow.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This diagnostic defeat explicitly isolates the decisive inference gap and states its consequence for the proposed identification of the cause.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move precisely distinguishes the formal Kalam conclusion from the additional transcendence, agency, and divine-identity claims.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is narrowly about what the stated syllogism entails, and its force matches the explicit difference between conclusion and add-on assertions.

charity.alternative: Further conceptual arguments after the Kalam syllogism could infer timelessness, immateriality, and agency without being premises of the syllogism itself.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those extensions must be independently defended; their absence from the bare syllogism does not alone prove them false.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The formal distinction is explicit and valid: a conclusion that there is a cause does not by itself entail the cause’s mentality or divinity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The stated premises and conclusion directly substantiate the entailment critique, with only the separate post-syllogism arguments left to examine.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central cosmic-cause bridge at the indispensable transition from an unspecified cause to a divine agent.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move correctly demands the added bridge, though calling the extensions merely glommed-on assertions slightly understates their possible independent defense.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt recites the Kalam’s conclusion that the universe had a cause and says transcendence and agency are additional assertions not contained in that argument.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: The resurrection's proposed minimal facts are not adequately confirmable data, and scholarly agreement, personal assessment, or sincerity cannot substitute for their underlying evidence.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker directly names Habermas and the minimal-facts approach while sustaining Dillahunty's first-person demand for data rather than assessments.

components.text: Whether the proposed minimal historical facts are confirmable enough to support a resurrection comparison.
Whether scholarly assessment and reported sincerity can substitute for the underlying historical data.

response.rationale: The move directly attacks the evidential foundation of the resurrection inference by distinguishing expert assessments from confirmable underlying data.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This full answer explicitly contacts the historical-premise demand, though it does not separately compare every resurrection alternative.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between data, scholarly assessment, and sincerity is consistently drawn and limited to evidential adequacy.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The demand for underlying evidence is well fitted, although saying the facts are unconfirmable is stronger than the excerpt’s detailed demonstration.

charity.alternative: Broad scholarly agreement can itself be evidence when specialists evaluate accessible historical sources and methods.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such agreement does not replace disclosure and assessment of the sources, independence, and warrants supporting the alleged facts.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference that explanatory comparison depends on adequately supported premises is explicit and sound, with a bounded gap about what counts as confirmation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies a real documentation requirement but does not itself systematically examine the sources underlying each proposed minimal fact.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central resurrection bridge by challenging the evidential status of the facts on which the best-explanation inference depends.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly distinguishes expert conclusions from raw evidence, though it gives limited credit to consensus as defeasible higher-order evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says the proposed minimal facts are not confirmable and rejects theologians’ or skeptics’ assessments as substitutes for data and evidence.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Demonstration requirements properly vary with the claim, so familiar ordinary claims need comparatively little support while worldview-altering claims require substantially stronger evidence.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty directly answers Hunter's request to define demonstration, using ordinary-dog and extraordinary-dragon examples to articulate his standard.

components.text: What level and type of evidence should be required for a worldview-altering resurrection claim.
Whether evidential demands may properly rise with the extraordinary scope of a divine-cause conclusion.

response.rationale: The reply answers the demand for a demonstration standard by explaining why evidential requirements vary with background knowledge and claim impact.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This full methodological answer clearly states the governing standard, though it does not operationalize the exact threshold for the debated claims.

precisionFindings.rationale: Ordinary and extraordinary claims are explicitly contrasted through background knowledge and potential worldview revision.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move advances a comparative evidential principle rather than an absolute threshold, and the dog-versus-dragon examples fit that limited force.

charity.alternative: Evidence should be evaluated by likelihood ratios and reliability, not simply by how psychologically worldview-altering a claim feels.
charity.decisiveQualification: Existing background knowledge and prior plausibility legitimately affect how much evidence is needed, even if subjective impact alone is insufficient.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative standard is coherent and avoids demanding certainty, with one bounded ambiguity between prior improbability and subjective worldview disruption.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The ordinary-dog and pet-dragon examples clearly illustrate background-sensitive evidence, though they do not specify a rigorous threshold for resurrection.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary provisional-inquiry bridge by articulating calibrated belief standards, while only indirectly testing particular central claims.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move captures the role of background knowledge but partly blends objective prior plausibility with a claim’s personal worldview impact.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts accepting an ordinary dog claim against demanding much more for a pet dragon because of background knowledge and worldview consequences.

moves.speaker: Braxton Hunter
moves.proposition: Requiring a science-like detector for God mistakes one reliable investigative method for a method capable of detecting every reality, whereas philosophy and history address different evidential domains.
moves.attributionBasis: The response is explicitly framed as Braxton's answer and develops his distinctive metal-detector analogy and philosophical case.

components.text: Whether the absence of a single science-like detector prevents reliable inquiry into God or historical events.
Whether philosophy and history can supply claim-appropriate evidence outside direct instrumental detection.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges method monism and identifies philosophy and history as domain-appropriate methods, while not fully answering source discrimination.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts the methodological-domain premise but leaves the decisive question of how those methods discriminate God from rival sources unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The metal-detector analogy clearly distinguishes a method’s reliability within one domain from universal scope across all realities.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Domain pluralism is well illustrated, but the further claim that philosophy reliably reaches the desired answers receives limited support in the excerpt.

charity.alternative: The skeptical demand is not necessarily for one universal detector but for each proposed method to discriminate divine claims from relevant alternatives.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing that multiple methods are legitimate does not show that the selected philosophical or historical method is reliable for this conclusion.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The anti-monism analogy is coherent, but it leaves a material bridge from domain appropriateness to the actual reliability and conclusions of philosophy and history.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The detector analogy supports limited methodological pluralism, while the reliability of the proposed philosophical and historical inferences is mostly asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It maximally contacts the subsidiary method-pluralism bridge by defending noninstrumental inquiry, though it does not complete the rival-discrimination requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The analogy fairly rejects universal instrumentalism but weakens the stronger discrimination challenge into excessive reliance on one detector.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt compares using a metal detector to deny sand, water, trees, and air, then identifies philosophy and history as different investigative means.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Even granting that the universe has a cause, the Kalam does not establish what that cause is or provide a method for knowing the attributes assigned to it.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt directly interrupts the claim that he offered no substantive Kalam response and states his own objection in first person.

components.text: Whether philosophy actually supplies a warranted method for knowing the universe cause’s assigned attributes.
Whether a cause of the universe is adequately identified as an agent or God.

response.rationale: The reply presses the exact epistemic gap left by method pluralism and the Kalam extension: what attributes follow and how they are known.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This full answer explicitly contacts the decisive reliability and attribute-identification demand, though it mainly poses the challenge rather than exhaustively rebutting each derivation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The concession of some cause is clearly separated from the disputed knowledge of that cause’s nature and attributes.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move conditionally grants a cause and proportionately demands warrants for additional attributes rather than claiming those attributes are impossible.

charity.alternative: Conceptual analysis of a cause of all physical spacetime may support some negative and modal attributes even without direct observation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Each positive step, especially mentality and agency, still requires a defended inference rather than a list of compatible descriptions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The underdetermination challenge is explicit and valid: accepting that a cause exists does not settle what it is or how its attributes are known.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The critique is grounded in the opponent’s acknowledged inferential extension, with a bounded omission because it does not examine every offered attribute argument.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central causal-underdetermination bridge at the indispensable transition from existence of a cause to knowledge of its nature.

representationalCharity.rationale: The conditional concession leaves room for conceptual inference while accurately focusing on the need to warrant each assigned attribute.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt conditionally grants a cause or explanation and asks what is known about that cause, how it is known, and whether the attributes are merely asserted.

moves.speaker: Braxton Hunter
moves.proposition: A timeless state producing the first temporal event is best explained by an agent with causal power and libertarian freedom rather than by an impersonal condition.
moves.attributionBasis: Braxton asks to answer the agency question and then presents the event-event, state-state, and state-event causation analysis.

components.text: How a timeless cause of the first temporal event can be identified as an agent rather than an impersonal state.
What independent post-Kalam argument supports adding agency to the bare causal conclusion.

response.rationale: The reply supplies the requested post-syllogism bridge through state-event causation and claims that voluntary agent causation explains temporal onset.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This full answer contacts the decisive attribute question and offers an inference, but does not adequately compare impersonal state-event alternatives.

precisionFindings.rationale: The state-event structure is recoverable, but “timeless nothingness,” causal power, and agent causation are not consistently or fully defined.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Saying agent causation is the only thing that makes sense radically narrows the alternatives beyond the abbreviated conceptual support supplied.

charity.alternative: An impersonal timeless condition could be sufficient only in conjunction with a boundary condition or non-temporal explanatory relation.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply must exclude such impersonal state-event models rather than rely on agent causation being the only familiar option.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Agent causation is compatible with the proposed onset, but compatibility is treated as unique explanation without a complete exclusion of impersonal conditions.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move offers a conceptual taxonomy but supplies little independent support for agent causation or representative comparison with competing state-event accounts.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central underdetermination bridge by attempting the indispensable agency inference, although the attempt remains materially incomplete.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents its agency model but largely dismisses the strongest impersonal alternative without a developed comparative argument.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt classifies the beginning as state-event causation, says only agent causation makes sense of it, and adds that the cause would require libertarian freedom.

moves.speaker: Braxton Hunter
moves.proposition: Divine foreknowledge does not eliminate libertarian freedom because knowing a person's future choice is not the same as causally determining that choice.
moves.attributionBasis: An audience member directs the question to Braxton, who explicitly answers it using the modal-fallacy and noncausal-knowledge distinction.

components.text: Whether divine knowledge of a future choice causally determines that choice and thereby removes freedom.
Whether divine selection of a complete foreknown world leaves genuine alternative possibilities available.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the foreknowledge-as-causation component but does not answer the distinct world-selection and fixed-history component of the objection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer squarely contacts a decisive component, while leaving the opponent’s stronger providential selection challenge unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between knowing a future act and efficiently causing it is clearly recoverable and consistently stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The narrow noncausation claim fits the conceptual distinction, though it does not establish the broader compatibility conclusion by itself.

charity.alternative: The objection can rest on divine world selection and the fixity of a fully foreknown history, not on knowledge being an efficient cause.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing that knowledge does not cause the choice leaves the modal and creative-selection challenge unresolved.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The knowledge-versus-causation distinction is valid, but a material bridge remains from noncausation to genuine alternative possibilities in a selected foreknown world.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinction supports the narrow answer, while no developed evidence or modal analysis addresses providence, prophecy, or world selection.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central agency-coherence bridge on foreknowledge, although it leaves another indispensable formulation of that bridge untouched.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply correctly answers a familiar causal reading but omits the strongest source-supported version involving selection of the complete history.

moves.evidenceBasis: The move frames the audience’s concern that omniscient knowledge makes the future already set and answers by distinguishing knowledge from causal determination.

moves.speaker: Braxton Hunter
moves.proposition: Christian theism is falsifiable through an internal contradiction or strong contrary historical evidence, although an apparent supernatural event associated with a rival religion would not by itself refute it.
moves.attributionBasis: The audience question is directed to Braxton, and his first-person answer continues through the locked lookahead with explicit falsification conditions.

components.text: Whether Christian theism admits conditions that could count against or falsify it.
What strength of contrary historical evidence could rationally overturn Christian theism.

response.rationale: The reply gives internal contradiction and strong contrary history as defeat conditions, while explaining that an isolated rival-associated anomaly is not uniquely decisive.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This full answer explicitly supplies falsification conditions, though their practical operationalization and the treatment of rival evidence remain compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed defeat conditions are clear, but “strong contrary historical evidence” remains broad and only partly operationalized.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move claims only that falsification routes exist and appropriately qualifies the evidential meaning of an isolated apparent rival miracle.

charity.alternative: A striking supernatural event tied to an incompatible religion could be substantial contrary evidence even if it were not deductively falsifying.
charity.decisiveQualification: Failure to entail Christianity’s falsity does not make such an event evidentially irrelevant to comparative worldview assessment.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Internal contradiction is a clear logical defeater and contrary history a coherent evidential defeater, with one ambiguity about comparative rather than deductive falsification.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conditions are conceptually plausible but remain general; no concrete threshold or developed example of sufficient historical defeat is provided.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly attacks the subsidiary method-reliability concern by identifying possible defeaters, while not resolving the central source-discrimination problem.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply properly distinguishes falsification from anomaly, but gives insufficient weight to the possible probabilistic force of rival religious evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines falsifiability and the locked proposition supplies internal contradiction and strong contrary historical evidence as possible defeaters, while qualifying rival supernatural events.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Beliefs are states of conviction rather than voluntary choices, although human decision-making also includes preferences and emotions that can serve rational and cooperative interests.
moves.attributionBasis: The question is expressly addressed to Matt, and the answer continues in a single first-person voice until Braxton is asked whether he wishes to follow up.

components.text: Whether people can freely choose the intellectual belief that is treated as a precondition for trusting God.
Whether all relevant human mental states and decisions exemplify libertarian voluntary choice.
Whether distinguishing causal determination from knowledge establishes voluntariness of belief.

response.rationale: The move directly challenges the voluntariness of belief and distinguishes conviction from broader decision-making, but does not address the modal foreknowledge reply.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts the belief-and-trust component and a secondary freedom claim, while leaving the principal foreknowledge analysis untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: Belief, preference, emotion, decision, and rational process are distinguished clearly enough to recover the limited voluntariness claim.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The introspective claim that beliefs are not chosen is plausible and qualified as the speaker’s view, but lacks broader empirical defense.

charity.alternative: People may indirectly influence belief through inquiry, attention, habits, and exposure even if conviction is not directly chosen.
charity.decisiveQualification: Indirect doxastic influence does not establish an immediate ability to choose sincere belief at will.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between conviction and voluntary action coherently rebuts direct doxastic voluntarism, with a bounded omission concerning indirect control.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The support is primarily introspective and conceptual, without representative psychological evidence, though ordinary inability to choose preferences is relevant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally challenges agency coherence where free trust presupposes voluntary belief, but does not defeat all libertarian action or foreknowledge claims.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move’s language concerns direct choice and remains compatible with substantial indirect influence over belief formation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says preferences and many decisions are not simply rational choices and explicitly states that beliefs are not choices.

moves.speaker: Braxton Hunter
moves.proposition: The raw number of New Testament variants is misleading when spread across thousands of manuscripts, and openly disclosed disputed passages do not by themselves establish pervasive textual corruption.
moves.attributionBasis: The answer follows Matt's remarks as the other debater's direct response and explicitly distinguishes agreement about known passages from disagreement about their broader significance.

components.text: Whether the large raw count of New Testament variants establishes pervasive textual uncertainty or corrupt revelation.
Whether openly identified disputed passages count as the kind of unclear disclosure predicted to be absent.
Whether manuscript abundance and disclosed variants establish the truth or divine source of Christian claims.

response.rationale: The reply contextualizes the variant count and known disputed passages, but does not establish divine source or answer the broader competing-revelation problem.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts the decisive textual-corruption component while leaving wider revelation inconsistency and source discrimination unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: Raw variants, manuscript count, words, disputed passages, and pervasive corruption are distinctly and consistently framed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move narrowly argues that raw counts are misleading and do not alone prove pervasive corruption, which fits the supplied numerical context.

charity.alternative: Many variants may still create uncertainty in particular consequential passages even when most arise from numerous manuscripts or minor differences.
charity.decisiveQualification: Contextualizing the aggregate count does not show that every doctrinally relevant reading is secure.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The denominator correction validly defeats the inference from a large aggregate count to every word being multiply uncertain, with a bounded doctrinal-security gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific counts of variants, words, and manuscripts directly support the contextual correction, though variant types and consequential readings are not surveyed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary text-and-miracle bridge by preserving textual credibility, while not completing the central revelation explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move limits its conclusion to what the raw count alone establishes and openly acknowledges disputed passages rather than denying all uncertainty.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts roughly 400,000 variants with about 138,000 New Testament words and explains that variants are distributed across more than 5,000 manuscripts.
